The peasant strains forward while the two riders sit comfortably above him.

explanation: Locked out of their meeting hall, the Third Estate's deputies swore the Tennis Court Oath not to separate until a constitution was written — the moment the revolution claimed sovereignty from the king.

option_explanations.A: The oath was defiance of the king, not loyalty to him; the raised arms pledge a constitution.
option_explanations.B: The oath came in June 1789; the king was not executed until 1793, and no such vote is depicted.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The unified raised arms and the president reading the pledge show the deputies committing to a constitution against royal wishes.
option_explanations.D: No declaration of war is shown; the scene is a political oath, and war came three years later.

options: (A) The deputies swore an oath of personal loyalty to Louis XVI, promising to defend his absolute authority against all challengers and to uphold the traditional social hierarchy of the three estates.
(B) The deputies voted to have the king executed.
(C) The deputies of the Third Estate pledged not to disband until they had written a constitution, directly challenging the king's authority.
(D) The deputies declared war on Austria and Prussia.
stem: What was the historical significance of the event depicted?
stimulus: Jacques-Louis David's large unfinished painting of the Tennis Court Oath, June 20, 1789: inside a crowded indoor tennis court, dozens of deputies stand with their right arms raised in unison toward the center, where the assembly's president, Bailly, stands on a table reading from a document. Light streams through high windows onto the raised arms of the crowd.

explanation: The Declaration's claims — liberty, property, legal equality, resistance to oppression, law as the general will — are textbook Enlightenment natural-rights ideas from thinkers like Locke, Montesquieu, and Rousseau.

option_explanations.A: The document limits royal power rather than defending divine right.
option_explanations.B: Mercantilism concerns trade policy, not the rights proclaimed here.
option_explanations.C: Napoleon came to power a decade later; the 1789 text predates him.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The tablet format itself echoes law-giving, and the content matches Enlightenment natural-rights philosophy.

options: (A) Medieval Catholic theology on the divine right of kings to rule without any limits.
(B) The economic doctrines of mercantilism, which taught that national wealth came from favorable trade balances and the accumulation of gold and silver in state treasuries.
(C) Napoleon's military maxims on centralized command and battlefield discipline.
(D) Enlightenment natural-rights philosophy, which held that liberty, property, and resistance to oppression belong to all men and that law expresses the general will.
stem: The principles proclaimed in this document drew most directly on which intellectual tradition?
stimulus: An engraved 1789 broadside of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen: the text is set on two stone tablets framed by classical columns, with allegorical winged figures above and the heading addressed 'Aux représentants du peuple français' (to the representatives of the French people).

explanation: By mirroring the men's declaration — 'representatives of the nation' demanding a national assembly — de Gouges exposed the contradiction of a revolution proclaiming universal rights while excluding women.

option_explanations.A: The text embraces revolutionary language ('assemblée nationale'), not royalism.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The deliberate echo of the 1789 declaration shows she is applying its universal claims to women.
option_explanations.C: The preamble demands women's political inclusion, the opposite of defending exclusion.
option_explanations.D: Women did not gain the vote in 1791; the pamphlet demands rights, not announces their grant.

options: (A) She opposed the French Revolution and wanted to restore the monarchy.
(B) She was turning the Revolution's own logic back on itself, demanding that the rights promised to 'men' in 1789 apply to women as well.
(C) She was defending the traditional exclusion of women from politics as natural and proper, arguing that women's place was in the home rather than in the assembly.
(D) She was announcing that women had already won the vote in 1791.
stem: What does the wording of this preamble reveal about the author's purpose?
stimulus: The first page of Olympe de Gouges's 1791 pamphlet, 'Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne.' Its preamble reads: 'Les mères, les filles, les soeurs, représentantes de la nation, demandent d'être constituées en assemblée nationale' (The mothers, daughters, and sisters, representatives of the nation, demand to be constituted as a national assembly).

explanation: The National Assembly — the Third Estate's deputies joined by reformers from the other orders — governed France in the king's name, marking the transfer of sovereignty from monarch to nation.

option_explanations.A: Correct. A large deliberative body legislating in public, watched by galleries, shows representative sovereignty replacing absolute monarchy.
option_explanations.B: The deputies were elected representatives, not royal appointees.
option_explanations.C: The Assembly voted by head, not by order; the separate-orders system had been abolished in 1789.
option_explanations.D: Napoleon's coronation was in 1804 in Notre-Dame, not a 1790 assembly hall.

options: (A) Sovereignty had shifted from the king ruling alone to a representative assembly claiming to speak for the nation.
(B) The king had personally appointed the deputies to advise him on financial matters, then dismissed them once they had approved his plan to raise new taxes.
(C) The assembly is shown voting by the three separate orders, as the Estates-General had traditionally done.
(D) The image shows Napoleon's coronation as emperor.
stem: What major political change is reflected in this image?
stimulus: An engraving of the National Assembly in session on February 4, 1790: a large hall filled with rows of seated deputies facing a central rostrum where a speaker stands, with crowded public galleries above watching the proceedings.

explanation: Corday — a Girondin sympathizer, not a royalist — was guillotined before a mass audience. The Terror made exemplary public execution the state's tool against political enemies of every stripe.

option_explanations.A: Victims of the Terror included nobles, clergy, and vast numbers of commoners; Corday herself was not nobility acting as such.
option_explanations.B: Corday assassinated Marat because she saw him as a radical tyrant; she supported the Girondin republicans, not the monarchy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The staged public spectacle of the guillotine in a renamed 'Revolution' square shows execution deployed as revolutionary justice.
option_explanations.D: The image itself, dated 1793, shows executions continuing well after 1789.

options: (A) The guillotine was used only against members of the nobility.
(B) Charlotte Corday was executed for being a secret royalist agent who had plotted with emigres to assassinate the republic's leaders.
(C) The revolutionary government used public execution as a political weapon against anyone it defined as an enemy of the revolution.
(D) Public executions had been abolished after 1789.
stem: What does this image best illustrate about the Reign of Terror?
stimulus: A 1793 engraving of the execution of Charlotte Corday in the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde): a large crowd surrounds the scaffold where the guillotine stands; carts and armed guards manage the dense onlookers gathered to watch the execution of the woman who had assassinated the radical leader Marat.

explanation: Gillray, a conservative satirist, portrays French revolutionaries as literal demons from hell (Pandaemonium) luring John Bull — propaganda expressing elite British fear of revolutionary contagion.

option_explanations.A: The revolutionaries are drawn as monsters, which is hostility, not support.
option_explanations.B: No alliance is shown; the French figures are menacing recruiters, not allies.
option_explanations.C: John Bull is being recruited by the French, not marching to invade them.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The demonic imagery and 'Recruiting Sarjeant' caption show a conservative warning that French radicalism threatened Britain.

options: (A) Gillray supported the French Revolution and urged Britons to join it.
(B) The cartoon celebrates a new military alliance between Britain and revolutionary France against their common continental rivals in central and eastern Europe.
(C) The cartoon shows British troops preparing to invade France.
(D) Conservative Britons feared revolutionary ideas would cross the Channel, and the cartoon mocks British radicals as dupes being recruited by French monsters.
stem: What does this British cartoon reveal about British attitudes toward the French Revolution in 1790?
stimulus: James Gillray's 1790 hand-colored cartoon 'Alecto and her train, at the gate of Pandaemonium': a monstrous fury labeled Alecto and a French drummer recruit a bewildered Englishman, 'John Bull,' into what the caption calls 'the Revolution Service,' while speech-filled papers swirl around them.

explanation: The 'bungling tinkers' metaphor — incompetent repairmen making the kettle worse — satirizes the Vienna diplomats as self-serving elites whose restoration settlement damaged Europe.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Calling the diplomats 'blockheads' who worsen the kettle's crack is contempt for their clumsy, self-interested redrawing of Europe.
option_explanations.B: The mocking caption and the image of a worsening crack are criticism, not praise.
option_explanations.C: Napoleon was exiled during the Congress; the figures are the allied diplomats.
option_explanations.D: The cartoon is dated 1815, the year of the Congress, not 1848.

options: (A) The cartoonist saw the diplomats as clumsy elites botching the restoration of Europe's monarchies out of self-interest.
(B) The cartoonist praised the Congress for skillfully rebuilding Europe.
(C) The cartoon shows Napoleon himself directing the settlement while the allied diplomats merely watch, take notes, and carry out his personal instructions.
(D) The cartoon depicts the revolutions of 1848.
stem: What view of the Congress of Vienna does this cartoon express?
stimulus: An 1815 British cartoon, 'The bungling tinkers, or Congress of blockheads': bewigged diplomats hammer and patch a large cracked kettle labeled as Europe, while the caption jeers that they have 'battered a hole in great Europe's kettle.'

explanation: The dancing circle mocks the diplomats as out-of-touch aristocrats waltzing while they restored monarchies and suppressed the nationalism and liberalism the revolutionary era had awakened.

option_explanations.A: The Congress restored monarchies; it granted no popular votes.
option_explanations.B: The figures dance in formal dress rather than planning war.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The festive, unserious dance contrasts with the grave business of redrawing nations, implying elite indifference to popular demands.
option_explanations.D: The caption names the Congress of Vienna (1814–1815), not the 1848 Frankfurt Parliament.

options: (A) It celebrates the Congress for giving ordinary people the vote.
(B) It shows the diplomats as military commanders planning a war.
(C) It portrays the peacemakers as frivolous elites who redrew Europe's borders to suit monarchs while ignoring liberal and nationalist demands.
(D) It depicts the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848, where German liberals gathered after the March revolutions to draft a constitution for a united, democratic German nation-state.
stem: Which criticism of the Vienna settlement is this caricature making?
stimulus: A French caricature captioned 'LE CONGRÈS': the great-power diplomats of the Congress of Vienna are drawn dancing together in a circle, arms linked, in festive dress, while Europe is rearranged around them.

explanation: Painted in 1851, the dramatic standing pose, flag, and dawn light are romantic invention, not documentation. The painting is excellent evidence of 19th-century nationalist memory — how Americans wanted to remember the founding — but weak evidence of the crossing itself.

option_explanations.A: Leutze painted in Germany in 1851, 75 years later; no one present at the crossing informed the work.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The theatrical composition made decades later reflects nationalist myth-making, so it reveals memory better than fact.
option_explanations.C: The crossing led to the American victory at Trenton, not a defeat.
option_explanations.D: The painting was commissioned for an American audience and celebrates the American cause.

options: (A) It is a primary source painted by an eyewitness to the crossing.
(B) It is more useful as evidence of how 19th-century Americans remembered and mythologized the Revolution than as a record of the 1776 crossing itself.
(C) It shows Washington's defeat at the Battle of Trenton.
(D) It was commissioned by the British government to mock the American cause, discourage further rebellion in the colonies, and celebrate British military superiority.
stem: A historian studying the American Revolution finds this image. What is the most careful conclusion she can draw about its value as evidence?
stimulus: Emanuel Leutze's 1851 painting 'Washington Crossing the Delaware': George Washington stands upright in the prow of a crowded rowboat pushing through ice chunks on a dark river at dawn, an American flag streaming behind him while soldiers strain at the oars around him. The scene is dramatic, heroic, and carefully composed — painted 75 years after the 1776 event.

explanation: The tea destruction dramatized the colonists' refusal to pay Parliament's tea tax — property destruction as political protest against taxation without representation.

option_explanations.A: The Tea Act of 1773 kept a tax on tea; it did not ban tea.
option_explanations.B: The figures dumping the tea are colonists, not a victorious British navy.
option_explanations.C: Parliament was the target of the protest, not its organizer.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The image shows colonists destroying taxed cargo to reject Parliament's authority to tax them.

options: (A) The colonists were protesting a British ban on all tea imports that threatened the livelihoods of colonial merchants.
(B) The image shows a British naval victory over French ships.
(C) The protest was organized and funded by the British Parliament.
(D) Colonists destroyed tea cargo to protest Parliament's claim to tax them without their consent.
stem: What does this image show about colonial resistance before 1776?
stimulus: A 19th-century print of the Boston Tea Party: under a moonlit sky, men in a harbor row alongside large sailing ships and heave wooden tea chests overboard into the water, where chests already float among the waves.

explanation: The 1840 engraving is a later commemoration — useful for studying 19th-century American memory of the founding, not the 1776 event's details.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Like Leutze's Washington, this is a 19th-century idealized commemoration; it reveals how Americans remembered the founding.
option_explanations.B: Photography did not exist in 1776, and the print is dated 1840.
option_explanations.C: The engraving is a composed scene, not proof of who was in the room on July 4.
option_explanations.D: The engraver's credit dates it to 1840, a bank-note company issue.

options: (A) It is a 19th-century idealized commemoration, best used as evidence of how later Americans remembered the founding rather than of the 1776 event itself.
(B) It is a photograph taken during the signing in 1776.
(C) It proves that every signer shown was present in the room on July 4, 1776, signed the document on that exact day, and personally witnessed the final vote.
(D) It was printed and distributed in Philadelphia in 1776.
stem: What does the date and style of this engraving tell a historian about how to use it?
stimulus: An 1840 engraving by the American Bank Note Company titled 'Signing the declaration of their independence': in a formal, well-lit assembly room, bewigged men in 18th-century dress gather around a central table signing a large document, arranged in a balanced, almost theatrical composition.

explanation: Bolívar was a creole — American-born of Spanish descent — and creole elites led most Spanish American independence movements, seeking political power matching their economic status.

option_explanations.A: Bolívar was a creole of Spanish descent, not an indigenous leader.
option_explanations.B: The uniform is that of a revolutionary general; the banner thanks him for liberating Peru from Spain.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Creole officers like Bolívar led the independence wars and adopted European military forms to legitimize their new states.
option_explanations.D: Bolívar dedicated his life to independence from Spain.

options: (A) Bolivar was an indigenous leader who rejected all European culture and military traditions, seeking instead to build a new state founded entirely on Native American customs and institutions.
(B) The portrait shows Bolivar as a loyal officer of the Spanish crown defending the empire.
(C) Bolivar was a creole elite whose military leadership of the independence wars reflects how American-born Spaniards, not the peninsulares, drove Spanish American independence.
(D) Bolivar opposed independence and fought to keep Peru under Spanish colonial rule.
stem: What does this portrait suggest about the social leadership of Latin American independence?
stimulus: José Gil de Castro's portrait of Simón Bolívar: Bolívar stands in full military dress — ornate gold-epauletted coat, white trousers, sword at his side — beneath a banner reading 'EL PERÚ RECONOCIDO A SIMÓN BOLÍVAR' (Peru grateful to Simón Bolívar), with a framed inscription below.

explanation: At Vertières (1803) Dessalines's Black army defeated the French; Haiti's 1804 independence made it the first Black republic and the only successful revolution by enslaved people.

option_explanations.A: The charging Black troops are defeating, not suffering defeat by, the French.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Vertières was the decisive Haitian victory that ended French rule and led to the 1804 founding of Haiti.
option_explanations.C: The image shows Haitian soldiers advancing as an organized army, not being crushed.
option_explanations.D: No American forces fought in Haiti; the combatants are Haitian and French.

options: (A) The image shows a French victory that restored slavery in Saint-Domingue, ended the Haitian rebellion for good, and returned the colony to profitable plantation production.
(B) The image shows Haitian forces defeating the French army, the decisive victory that made Haiti the first independent Black republic founded by formerly enslaved people.
(C) The image shows a slave revolt being crushed by colonial militia.
(D) The image shows American troops aiding the French in Haiti.
stem: Why is the battle shown here historically significant?
stimulus: An engraving of the Battle of Vertières, 1803: Black Haitian soldiers in military uniforms charge forward with muskets and bayonets against French troops, who fall back amid smoke and fallen bodies. The Haitian attackers advance in disciplined formation.

explanation: Raffet shows Haitian troops as a real army storming fortifications — the revolution was waged by organized Black soldiers who defeated Europe's armies.

option_explanations.A: The image depicts an intense assault, not a bloodless victory.
option_explanations.B: The attackers are Black Haitian troops, not French colonists.
option_explanations.C: The uniforms, fort, and landscape are Haitian, not North American.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The disciplined assault shows the Haitian revolution as a war fought by organized formerly enslaved soldiers.

options: (A) Haitians won independence without any fighting.
(B) The image shows French colonists bravely defending their plantations against a disorganized mob of rebels with no military training or leadership.
(C) The image depicts a battle of the American Revolution.
(D) Formerly enslaved Haitians fought as organized armies using both conventional assaults and guerrilla tactics to defeat French forces.
stem: What does this image demonstrate about how the Haitian Revolution was fought?
stimulus: Auguste Raffet's colored engraving of the combat and capture of Crête-à-Pierrot: Black Haitian soldiers swarm up a fortified hillside toward a French-held fort, firing muskets as French defenders resist; bodies lie on the slope beneath drifting smoke.

explanation: Napoleon dispatched General Leclerc's 1802 expedition to retake Saint-Domingue and restore slavery (abolished 1794). Toussaint's arrest and the war's renewal led directly to Haitian independence.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The 1802 Leclerc expedition aimed to reimpose French control and slavery, which reignited full-scale war.
option_explanations.B: The fleet came to crush the Black leadership, not to free the colony.
option_explanations.C: The ships fly French flags; the expedition was French.
option_explanations.D: The Louisiana Purchase was a separate 1803 diplomatic sale, not a military landing.

options: (A) Napoleon sent a French army to retake Saint-Domingue and restore slavery, which provoked the renewed war that ended in Haitian independence.
(B) The French fleet arrived to grant Saint-Domingue its independence peacefully.
(C) The image shows British troops landing to aid the Haitian rebels.
(D) The image depicts the American purchase of Louisiana from France in 1803, a peaceful diplomatic transaction negotiated by President Jefferson's envoys in Paris.
stem: What was the purpose of the expedition shown in this image?
stimulus: An engraving of the French fleet disembarking at Saint-Domingue in 1802: warships crowd the harbor while rowboats ferry uniformed French soldiers ashore amid cannon smoke, as the expedition moves against the colony's Black forces.

explanation: Born enslaved, Toussaint became the revolution's general and governor; the French-style uniform in his portrait asserts his status as a legitimate military and political leader.

option_explanations.A: Toussaint was born enslaved in Saint-Domingue and rose through the revolution.
option_explanations.B: Toussaint led the forces that ended slavery in the colony; he did not oppose abolition.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The epaulettes and uniform present him as a commanding general, claiming the authority of a head of state.
option_explanations.D: Toussaint died in a French prison in 1803, not by execution in 1791.

options: (A) Toussaint was a French-born officer sent from Paris to govern the colony, suppress the slave rebellion there, and restore the plantation economy to full production under the old system.
(B) Toussaint opposed the abolition of slavery in Saint-Domingue.
(C) Toussaint rose from enslavement to command the colony's armies, and his European-style general's uniform projects his claim to legitimate authority.
(D) Toussaint was executed by the revolutionaries in 1791.
stem: What does this portrait reveal about Toussaint Louverture's historical role?
stimulus: An engraving labeled 'Toussaint L'Ouverture': a Black man in a French general's uniform with heavy epaulettes and a sash gazes directly at the viewer, his hand resting on his sword hilt.

explanation: The 1806 print dresses the Black liberator in the full regalia of European power — plumed hat, sash, sword — while the tropical backdrop marks his Haitian domain: a visual argument that Black sovereignty deserved the same recognition as European states.

option_explanations.A: The dress is European military, not traditional African clothing.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The portrait deliberately fuses European symbols of command with a Black leader to demand recognition of his authority.
option_explanations.C: By 1806 Toussaint was Napoleon's prisoner; the print celebrates his leadership, not loyalty to France.
option_explanations.D: The heroic full-length format honors rather than mocks him.

options: (A) It shows Toussaint wearing traditional African royal dress and ceremonial ornaments.
(B) The artist blends European symbols of military power with Toussaint's identity as a Black leader, projecting sovereignty to both European and Haitian viewers.
(C) It proves that Toussaint remained a loyal general serving Napoleon throughout his entire career, carrying out orders from Paris faithfully from his first commission to his final day.
(D) It is a British caricature mocking Toussaint's pretensions to grandeur and authority.
stem: What is the artist communicating through the combination of European military dress and the tropical landscape?
stimulus: A 1806 engraving, 'Toussaint Louverture': a full-length portrait of a Black man in an ornate plumed hat, braided military coat, sash, and sword, holding official papers, with a tropical mountain landscape behind him and his name engraved below.

explanation: The Code civil standardized law across Napoleon's empire — equality before the law, property rights, religious toleration — while entrenching his authoritarian, patriarchal rule.

option_explanations.A: The Code abolished feudal privileges and standardized law; it did not restore them.
option_explanations.B: The title page dates it to 1804 (Year XII), after the revolution.
option_explanations.C: It was imposed across France and Napoleon's satellite states, not just Paris.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 'official edition' title page shows the state publishing one uniform law code — a lasting Napoleonic reform.

options: (A) It restored feudal law and noble privilege.
(B) It was written before the French Revolution.
(C) It applied only within the city of Paris and was never enforced anywhere else in France or in the conquered satellite states of the Napoleonic empire at all.
(D) Napoleon's regime imposed a single uniform legal code, spreading legal equality and property rights while consolidating centralized authoritarian rule.
stem: What does this title page reveal about Napoleon's government?
stimulus: The title page of the 1804 'Code civil des Français': 'CODE CIVIL DES FRANÇAIS. ÉDITION ORIGINALE ET SEULE OFFICIELLE. À PARIS, DE L'IMPRIMERIE DE LA RÉPUBLIQUE. AN XII. — 1804,' beneath an allegorical female figure of Justice with scales.

explanation: Watt's efficient engine decoupled industry from rivers: factories could be built near coal, labor, and markets, run all year, and power many machines — the core of the factory system.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Steam freed factories from water-power sites, enabling year-round urban industry near coal and workers.
option_explanations.B: Many machines predated Watt; his engine was a major improvement, not the first machine ever.
option_explanations.C: The diagram shows a boiler, piston, and flywheel — coal-fired steam, not electricity.
option_explanations.D: In 1780 the engine powered mines and mills; steam locomotives came later.

options: (A) Steam power freed factories from rivers, so industry could locate near coal and labor and operate year-round, making the factory system possible.
(B) It was the very first machine ever invented by humans in all of recorded history, with no earlier mechanical devices of any kind whatsoever existing before it.
(C) It was powered by electricity.
(D) In 1780 it was used mainly to pull railroad trains.
stem: Why was the machine shown here so important to industrialization?
stimulus: A labeled 1780 diagram of Watt's steam engine: a massive rocking beam connects a brick-encased boiler and piston on one side to a large flywheel on the other, with rods, valves, and a governor drawn in careful engineering detail.

explanation: The jenny's many spindles let one worker spin many threads at once — productivity per worker soared, drawing textile work out of cottages into factories.

option_explanations.A: Early jennies were hand-powered; steam came later.
option_explanations.B: The jenny increased cotton consumption; it did not reduce raw-material needs.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Multiple spindles per worker multiplied output and made centralized factory production economical.
option_explanations.D: The jenny spun thread; it had nothing to do with ships.

options: (A) It was powered by a steam engine from the day it was invented.
(B) It reduced the amount of raw cotton textile makers needed.
(C) It let one worker spin many threads at once, multiplying output per worker and pulling textile production from cottages into factories.
(D) It was invented in the 1760s to manufacture heavy canvas sails for the warships of the British Royal Navy during its naval arms race with France.
stem: What economic change does this machine best illustrate?
stimulus: An 1836 Penny Magazine engraving of Hargreaves's spinning jenny: a long wooden frame holds rows of upright spindles, turned by a single large wheel at one end, with a moving carriage — one operator could work many spindles simultaneously.

explanation: The Liverpool–Manchester line (1830) proved railways could move bulk goods fast and cheaply, knitting regions into national markets and accelerating industrial growth.

option_explanations.A: The vehicle shown is a steam locomotive on rails, decades before the automobile.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Cheap, fast overland transport integrated markets and spread industrialization.
option_explanations.C: Passenger excursion traffic mattered, but freight and market integration were the main economic effects.
option_explanations.D: The rails, locomotive, and triumphal arch show a railway, not a canal.

options: (A) It shows the first successful gasoline-powered automobile, which within a few years replaced all horse-drawn transport throughout England.
(B) Railways drastically cut the cost and time of moving goods overland, integrating national markets and accelerating industrialization.
(C) Railways were built mainly as amusements for wealthy leisure travelers.
(D) It depicts the opening of a new canal.
stem: What was the most important economic effect of the development shown here?
stimulus: A print of the 1830 opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway: a steam locomotive pulls carriages beneath a decorated triumphal arch while enormous crowds line the tracks and wave flags.

explanation: The gin made short-staple upland cotton profitable, so cotton cultivation — and with it slavery — exploded across the Deep South. A labor-saving invention intensified coerced labor.

option_explanations.A: The gin made cotton enormously profitable, which expanded slavery rather than ending it.
option_explanations.B: Whitney was an American; the patent is American (1794).
option_explanations.C: The gin separated seeds from cotton fiber, not wool.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The patent drawing's mechanical separator made upland cotton profitable, driving the westward expansion of plantation slavery.

options: (A) It made cotton unprofitable and helped end slavery.
(B) It was invented in Britain to process raw Indian cotton for the great mechanized textile mills of Lancashire and Manchester, replacing American supplies.
(C) It was designed to process wool.
(D) By making short-staple cotton profitable, the gin caused cotton cultivation and slavery to expand enormously across the American South.
stem: What was the most significant unintended consequence of the invention shown in this patent drawing?
stimulus: Eli Whitney's 1794 U.S. patent drawing for the cotton gin, marked '72X': labeled mechanical views (Fig. 1 through Fig. 4) show a toothed cylinder and grate system designed to pull cotton fibers through while leaving the seeds behind.

explanation: The mocking 'Leader of the Luddites' cartoon shows machine-breakers in action: workers who smashed textile machinery blamed it for unemployment and falling wages.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The cartoon's broken frames and crowd show workers destroying machines they blamed for lost jobs.
option_explanations.B: Luddites targeted machinery, not the monarchy.
option_explanations.C: The exaggerated, ragged 'leader' is drawn to ridicule, not to praise.
option_explanations.D: Luddism was an English movement (1811–1816), not French.

options: (A) Some British textile workers smashed the new machines, blaming mechanization for unemployment and lower wages.
(B) Luddites were revolutionaries trying to overthrow the British monarchy.
(C) The cartoonist supported the Luddites and celebrated their leader as a working-class hero fighting for justice.
(D) The Luddites were French revolutionaries who invaded England.
stem: What historical development does this cartoon depict?
stimulus: A hand-colored cartoon titled 'THE LEADER OF THE LUDDITES': a ragged, wild-eyed figure gestures commandingly while behind him a crowd attacks and smashes wooden textile frames, with broken machinery scattered on the ground.

explanation: Lowell's young women operatives — America's first large female industrial workforce — organized for shorter hours and better conditions, showing industrialization creating new worker identities and collective action.

option_explanations.A: The constitution is written by and for the operatives themselves, not the owners.
option_explanations.B: It is a workers' association document, not state legislation.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The printed constitution shows mill women formally organizing — an early American labor organization born of factory life.
option_explanations.D: The association was formed by employed mill women to improve their conditions, not to oppose women's work.

options: (A) It shows a set of strict disciplinary rules imposed on workers by factory owners to control their behavior, limit their wages, and punish any disobedience harshly with fines.
(B) It was written by the Massachusetts state legislature.
(C) Young women mill workers formed one of America's early labor organizations, showing how factory work created a new wage-earning class that organized collectively.
(D) It shows an organization opposed to women working in factories.
stem: What does this document reveal about the social effects of industrialization?
stimulus: A printed broadside, 'CONSTITUTION OF THE Lowell Factory Girls Association': a formal preamble and numbered articles organize the women operatives of Lowell's textile mills into an association with officers, dues, and stated purposes.

explanation: The flyer's language — 'slaves of capital,' 'political serfs' — and its call for a peaceful mass procession show industrial workers organizing to demand the vote.

option_explanations.A: The flyer's motto is 'PEACE and ORDER,' explicitly rejecting violence.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The flyer mobilizes working men around political demands, chiefly the franchise.
option_explanations.C: The flyer demands reform; it does not oppose it.
option_explanations.D: The flyer is addressed 'TO THE WORKING MEN OF LONDON' by a workers' committee.

options: (A) Chartists demanded a violent revolution to overthrow Parliament.
(B) Industrial workers organized mass peaceful demonstrations to demand political rights, above all the right to vote.
(C) The Chartists opposed all political reform and wanted to preserve the existing aristocratic system completely unchanged forever.
(D) The flyer was issued by factory owners to discourage unions.
stem: What does this flyer show about working-class politics in industrial Britain?
stimulus: An 1848 flyer headlined 'CHARTIST DEMONSTRATION!!' declaring '"PEACE and ORDER" is our MOTTO!' It addresses 'THE WORKING MEN OF LONDON': 'We are the slaves of capital... We are political serfs,' and calls them to 'join in our peaceful procession on MONDAY NEXT, April 10' from several London meeting points 'to Kennington Common.'

explanation: In 1819 cavalry charged a peaceful reform meeting at St. Peter's Field, Manchester, killing demonstrators — authorities' violent answer to demands for parliamentary reform.

option_explanations.A: The scene is a domestic crowd in Manchester, not a foreign battlefield.
option_explanations.B: The crowd holds banners and is being ridden down; the violence comes from the cavalry.
option_explanations.C: The banners, dress, and dedication to Henry Hunt place it in England, 1819.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mounted troops attacking a banner-carrying reform crowd shows the state's violent repression of peaceful demands.

options: (A) It celebrates a glorious British military victory over Napoleon's armies on a distant foreign battlefield during the Napoleonic Wars, honoring the brave fallen heroes.
(B) It shows an armed crowd attacking government troops.
(C) It depicts a battle of the French Revolution.
(D) British authorities used military force against peaceful demonstrators demanding parliamentary reform, revealing elite fear of revolution after 1815.
stem: What does this image reveal about Britain's response to demands for reform after the Napoleonic Wars?
stimulus: Richard Carlile's 1819 engraving of the Peterloo Massacre: mounted soldiers with raised sabers charge into a dense crowd of civilians carrying reform banners (one addressed 'To Henry Hunt, Esq.'), trampling men and women as onlookers flee.

explanation: The League — backed by manufacturers — argued the Corn Laws raised bread prices to protect landlords; repeal (1846) was a victory for free trade and middle-class political power.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The packed meeting shows a middle-class free-trade campaign against agricultural tariffs that kept food prices high.
option_explanations.B: The League was a middle-class manufacturers' movement; the vote was the Chartists' cause.
option_explanations.C: The League campaigned to repeal tariffs, not raise them.
option_explanations.D: The image shows a political meeting hall, not a religious service.

options: (A) Middle-class manufacturers organized to repeal grain tariffs, arguing the Corn Laws raised food prices to protect landowners, a free-trade campaign.
(B) Workers met to demand universal male suffrage.
(C) Landowners met to demand higher tariffs on imported grain.
(D) The image shows a religious revival meeting led by evangelical preachers calling for moral reform, temperance, and Sabbath observance among the working classes.
stem: What movement does this image document, and what did it want?
stimulus: An 1846 print of an 'Anti-Corn Law League Meeting': a grand hall packed with hundreds of well-dressed attendees facing a central platform, banners and a formal, orderly assembly.

explanation: Wedgwood mass-produced the medallion so ordinary buyers could wear abolitionism — an early cause marketed through consumer goods, making moral opposition to slavery fashionable and visible.

option_explanations.A: The medallion was designed by a white artist and made in Wedgwood's English factory.
option_explanations.B: The kneeling figure and plea argue against slavery, not for the trade.
option_explanations.C: Correct. A fashionable ceramic medallion let consumers display abolitionist sympathy — moral persuasion through mass-produced goods.
option_explanations.D: It is a jasperware medallion, not currency, and it was made to oppose slavery.

options: (A) It was carved by enslaved artisans in the Caribbean.
(B) It was produced to advertise the slave trade to wealthy investors, merchants, and plantation owners in Britain and the Caribbean colonies as a respectable business.
(C) Abolitionists spread their message through fashionable mass-produced consumer goods, letting ordinary buyers publicly display opposition to slavery.
(D) It is a coin that was used to purchase enslaved people.
stem: What does this object reveal about abolitionist strategy in late-18th-century Britain?
stimulus: A photograph of a Wedgwood jasperware medallion (c. 1787): a kneeling Black man in chains raises his hands, encircled by the words 'AM I NOT A MAN AND A BROTHER.'

explanation: The Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade published the plan to visualize the Middle Passage — rows of bodies packed like cargo made the trade's cruelty undeniable to Parliament and the public.

option_explanations.A: The diagram was created by abolitionists to attack the trade, not by captains to promote it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The packed human figures turned abstract suffering into a concrete image that fueled abolitionist campaigns.
option_explanations.C: The bodies are packed far tighter than any humane limit; the image argues the opposite.
option_explanations.D: The labeled decks, hatches, and human cargo identify it as a slave ship.

options: (A) It was drawn by a slave-ship captain to attract investors to the trade.
(B) Abolitionists published the diagram to make the Middle Passage's inhumanity visible and concrete, building public support for ending the trade.
(C) It shows that slavers respected legal limits on how many people they carried.
(D) It depicts a heavily armed British warship of the Royal Navy on patrol against the pirates and privateers operating along the Atlantic Ocean trade routes.
stem: Why did abolitionists circulate images like this one?
stimulus: 'Description of a Slave Ship' (British Library): detailed deck plans of the slave ship Brookes show cross-sections and top-down views in which every deck is filled with rows of small drawn human figures packed shoulder-to-shoulder and head-to-toe, each figure labeled.

explanation: The poster's own headline — 'under the regulated slave trade' — concedes Parliament had begun regulating but not abolishing; abolitionists used the regulated stowage plan to prove the trade was unreformable.

option_explanations.A: Packing hundreds of people into a hull is shown as brutal, not humane.
option_explanations.B: The poster was abolitionist propaganda attacking the trade, not celebrating it.
option_explanations.C: The slave trade was not abolished until 1807; regulation came first.
option_explanations.D: Correct. 'Regulated' reveals the intermediate stage — Parliament limiting the trade before abolishing it — and the diagram argued regulation could not make it humane.

options: (A) The poster proves that conditions on slave ships were comfortable and well regulated by law, showing that Parliament's rules had ended all suffering and made the Middle Passage a safe and humane journey for everyone aboard.
(B) It was issued by slave traders to celebrate their business and attract new investors.
(C) It shows that the slave trade had already been completely abolished by Parliament.
(D) It shows an intermediate stage in which Parliament regulated but had not yet abolished the trade, and abolitionists used the official stowage plan to argue the trade was inherently inhumane.
stem: What does the wording of this poster's headline tell a historian about the state of the abolition campaign?
stimulus: A printed poster titled 'STOWAGE OF THE BRITISH SLAVE SHIP BROOKES UNDER THE REGULATED SLAVE TRADE': cross-sections and deck plans show tightly packed rows of enslaved people, accompanied by tables and explanatory text.

explanation: Crowe, an English artist touring the South in the 1850s, painted enslaved people held in a Richmond pen awaiting auction — documenting the domestic trade's commodification of human beings on the eve of the Civil War.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The seated, waiting figures and inspecting buyers show enslaved people treated as merchandise in the 1850s South.
option_explanations.B: The figures are confined in a pen awaiting sale, not free workers.
option_explanations.C: Richmond, Virginia, is in the American South, not the Caribbean.
option_explanations.D: Crowe painted it in the 1850s–1861, just before the Civil War.

options: (A) The image documents the domestic slave trade's dehumanization, enslaved people displayed and inspected like goods, persisting in the American South into the 1860s.
(B) It shows freed Black workers happily attending a crowded public job fair to find paid employment in the hopeful years immediately after emancipation was declared across the South.
(C) It depicts enslaved laborers on a Caribbean sugar plantation.
(D) It was painted before 1800.
stem: What does this painting document about slavery in the United States?
stimulus: Eyre Crowe's 1861 painting 'Slaves Waiting for Sale, Richmond, Virginia': inside a dim slave pen, Black men, women, and children sit on benches while white buyers walk among them, inspecting them as if they were merchandise.

explanation: Schoelcher's annotated draft — 'slavery is an attack on human dignity' — became the April 1848 decree by which France's Second Republic abolished slavery in its colonies.

option_explanations.A: Napoleon restored slavery in 1802; the 1848 decree reversed that.
option_explanations.B: The decree abolished slavery in the colonies; metropolitan France had no slaves to free.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The draft's language and 1848 date show the revolutionary government deliberately applying 'liberty, equality, fraternity' to enslaved colonial subjects.
option_explanations.D: The manuscript is dated 1848, not 1789.

options: (A) Napoleon personally issued this sweeping 1848 decree to abolish slavery throughout the entire French colonial empire as a deliberate act of revolutionary justice and reform.
(B) The decree applied only within France itself.
(C) France's 1848 revolutionary government abolished slavery in the French colonies, extending revolutionary ideals of liberty and equality to enslaved people.
(D) The decree was issued during the first French Revolution in 1789.
stem: What does this document represent in the history of abolition?
stimulus: Victor Schoelcher's handwritten, annotated 1848 draft of the abolition decree: headed 'République française. Liberté — Égalité — Fraternité. Au nom du Peuple français,' it declares 'Considérant que l'esclavage est un attentat contre la dignité humaine...' (Considering that slavery is an attack on human dignity...).

explanation: Alexander II emancipated the serfs by imperial decree in 1861 — reform from above meant to preserve autocracy and modernize the army and economy — but redemption payments and the commune kept peasants economically bound.

option_explanations.A: The manifesto was read by a priest as an imperial decree; no peasant revolt forced it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The top-down, officially staged reading shows emancipation as the tsar's gift — legal freedom paired with economic obligations that preserved much of the old order.
option_explanations.C: Peasants had to pay redemption dues for decades; the land settlement was far from free and full.
option_explanations.D: The tsar remained firmly on the throne; the monarchy lasted until 1917.

options: (A) Russian peasants won emancipation through a successful revolt.
(B) The tsar freed the serfs from above to preserve autocracy and modernize Russia, but redemption payments kept peasants economically tied to the land.
(C) The decree gave peasants full, free, and unconditional ownership of all the land they worked, with no redemption payments of any kind ever required from them whatsoever.
(D) The decree abolished the Russian monarchy.
stem: What does this image reveal about the character of Russian emancipation?
stimulus: An official painting of the emancipation of the serfs in 1861: a priest in ornate robes reads the imperial manifesto from a paper to a large, solemn crowd of bearded Russian peasants gathered around him.

explanation: The Seneca Falls reformers consciously echoed 1776 — 'all men and women are created equal' — to claim natural rights for women, linking abolitionism and women's rights.

option_explanations.A: Both 'LADIES' and 'GENTLEMEN' columns appear; Frederick Douglass is among the gentlemen.
option_explanations.B: The convention was organized by women reformers, not by Congress.
option_explanations.C: Most organizers were abolitionists; the card's signer list includes the Black abolitionist Frederick Douglass.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The card's title and the convention's text deliberately mirror the Declaration of Independence to demand women's equality.

options: (A) Every single one of the signers was a woman, and absolutely no men participated in, attended, or supported the convention in any public way whatsoever.
(B) The convention was organized by the United States Congress.
(C) The signers opposed the abolition of slavery.
(D) American women reformers modeled their demands on the Declaration of Independence, claiming the natural rights of 1776 applied to women as well.
stem: What strategy does this card show the Seneca Falls reformers using?
stimulus: A printed 'Roll of Honor' card for the Woman's Rights Convention at Seneca Falls, New York, July 19–20, 1848: it lists the signers of the Declaration of Sentiments in two columns, 'LADIES' and 'GENTLEMEN' — the gentlemen's column including the abolitionist Frederick Douglass.

explanation: Wollstonecraft's 1792 Vindication argued that women, given equal education, were equally rational — applying Enlightenment reason to attack the idea of natural female inferiority.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Wollstonecraft used Enlightenment arguments about reason and natural rights to demand women's education and equality.
option_explanations.B: She welcomed the French Revolution and applied its principles to women.
option_explanations.C: Her argument was for universal rights; she did not defend slavery.
option_explanations.D: Women could not sit in Parliament in the 1790s; she was a writer, not an MP.

options: (A) She argued that Enlightenment ideas of reason and natural rights applied to women, and that equal education would prove women's equal rational capacity.

(B) She opposed the French Revolution as a dangerous threat to tradition and the established social order, and urged Britain to strengthen the monarchy and the established church against all democratic reforms.
(C) She wrote pamphlets in defense of slavery and the colonial plantation system.
(D) She served as an elected member of the British Parliament representing London.
stem: Mary Wollstonecraft, shown here, is best known for which argument?
stimulus: A portrait after John Opie's 1797 painting of Mary Wollstonecraft, the English writer whose 1792 book 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' responded to the French Revolution's talk of universal rights.

explanation: Article X's logic — equal punishment implies equal rights — was precisely the revolutionary universalism the male leadership refused to apply; de Gouges was guillotined in 1793.

option_explanations.A: The Assembly never adopted her declaration; women's political clubs were soon suppressed.
option_explanations.B: The plaque reproduces her demand for equal rights; she was its author, not its opponent.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Her articles apply the Revolution's universal logic to women — a claim the revolutionary government rejected, executing her in 1793.
option_explanations.D: The declaration was written in 1791, during the first revolution.

options: (A) The National Assembly adopted her declaration as law in 1791.
(B) Olympe de Gouges opposed women's rights.
(C) De Gouges used the Revolution's own principle of equality to demand women's rights, but the revolutionary leadership rejected her claims and she was executed in 1793.

(D) The declaration was actually written much later, during the revolution of 1848, nearly sixty years after the first French Revolution had ended and Napoleon's empire had completely fallen from power.
stem: What does this text reveal about the limits of the French Revolution's universalism?
stimulus: A Paris memorial plaque reproducing Olympe de Gouges's 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman: its articles declare women's equal natural rights, including Article X — 'Woman has the right to mount the scaffold; she must equally have the right to mount the rostrum' (to speak in public and govern).

explanation: Garibaldi's redshirt volunteers — the Thousand who sailed to Sicily in 1860 — show Italian unification as a popular nationalist crusade, not only Piedmontese statecraft.

option_explanations.A: Garibaldi fought for Italian unification, not for France.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The volunteer redshirts boarding boats show nationalism mobilizing ordinary Italians for unification.
option_explanations.C: The Thousand sailed from Genoa to Sicily, not to America.
option_explanations.D: Garibaldi was unification's most famous popular champion.

options: (A) Garibaldi fought as a general for the French army against the Austrians in the wars of northern Italy, seeking to expand French territory at Italy's expense.
(B) Italian unification drew on popular nationalist volunteers as well as state power, as the redshirted Thousand sailing to liberate the south shows.
(C) The Thousand sailed to the Americas.
(D) Garibaldi opposed Italian unification.
stem: What does this image show about the forces behind Italian unification?
stimulus: An 1860 print of Garibaldi departing on the Expedition of the Thousand: Garibaldi in his red shirt directs redshirted volunteers as they board small boats at the shore, with ships waiting offshore.

explanation: Proclaiming the German Empire in Louis XIV's palace — just after defeating France — was staged to symbolize German military triumph and French humiliation, cementing Prussian-led unification.

option_explanations.A: The scene is a triumphant proclamation, not a defeat.
option_explanations.B: The uniforms, banners, and 1871 date place it at Versailles after the Franco-Prussian War, not Frankfurt in 1848.
option_explanations.C: The emperor is proclaimed by princes and generals, not crowned by popular vote.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Holding the ceremony in the defeated enemy's palace advertised that German unity was won by Prussian arms at France's expense.

options: (A) It shows Germany's defeat in war.
(B) It depicts the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848.
(C) It shows Wilhelm I being crowned by a direct popular vote of the German people in a grand, peaceful democratic ceremony celebrating German national unity, freedom, and self-determination.
(D) Staging the proclamation in the French king's palace was a deliberate symbol of German victory and French humiliation, cementing unification under Prussian leadership.
stem: Why was the location of the event shown here significant?
stimulus: Anton von Werner's painting of the proclamation of the German Empire: on January 18, 1871, in the glittering Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, Wilhelm I of Prussia is hailed as German Emperor before an assembly of German princes and uniformed officers.

explanation: Duncan's print shows British steam-and-sail warships annihilating Chinese junks — the industrial military gap that forced China to sign the Treaty of Nanjing (1842), opening ports and ceding Hong Kong.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The one-sided naval destruction shows the industrial power gap that let Britain impose the 'unequal treaties' on China.
option_explanations.B: The burning, sinking junks are Chinese; Britain won the war.
option_explanations.C: The flags and 1843 date place it in the First Opium War, not the 1890s Sino-Japanese War.
option_explanations.D: Britain was the aggressor, forcing the opium trade on China.

options: (A) Britain's industrial-era naval superiority let it defeat China and force open Chinese ports to foreign trade after the Treaty of Nanjing.
(B) China won the Opium War decisively, expelled the British from Chinese waters for good, and permanently closed its ports to all foreign trade forever.
(C) The image shows the Sino-Japanese War.
(D) Britain was defending itself against a Chinese invasion.
stem: What does this image reveal about the global balance of power in the mid-19th century?
stimulus: E. Duncan's 1843 print of the First Opium War: British warships with billowing sails fire broadsides into Chinese war junks, whose masts collapse in flames and smoke as the wooden vessels break apart.

explanation: The 1857 engraving shows Indian sepoys attacking the British Redan battery at Lucknow — part of the great anti-colonial uprising Britain crushed, then used to justify replacing Company rule with direct Crown control.

option_explanations.A: The attackers are Indians assaulting a British position, not a British celebration.
option_explanations.B: The attackers are Indian sepoys and rebels, not French troops.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The image shows the scale of the 1857 anti-British revolt, after which Britain imposed direct Crown rule over India.
option_explanations.D: The uniforms, setting, and 1857 date place it in India, not America.

options: (A) It shows a British victory celebration.
(B) The attackers are French troops.
(C) The image shows Indian soldiers and rebels attacking British positions in the 1857 uprising, the anti-colonial revolt that led Britain to impose direct Crown rule over India.
(D) It depicts a dramatic and bloody battle of the American Civil War in 1862 between Union and Confederate armies fiercely fighting over a heavily fortified earthwork position in Virginia.
stem: What historical development does this image depict?
stimulus: An 1857 engraving titled 'Attack of the Mutineers on the Redan Battery at Lucknow, July 30th, 1857': Indian sepoys in turbans and uniforms storm a British defensive earthwork, scaling its walls as British defenders fire back through smoke.

explanation: Delacroix painted the July Revolution of 1830 — Parisians toppling Charles X — using Liberty as an allegorical woman with Phrygian cap and tricolor. Students often misdate it to 1789.

option_explanations.A: The painting is dated 1830 and shows the July Revolution, not the 1789 Bastille.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Delacroix commemorated the 1830 overthrow of Charles X, using the female Liberty — Phrygian cap, tricolor, musket — as revolutionary allegory.
option_explanations.C: It was painted in 1830, eighteen years before the 1848 revolution.
option_explanations.D: Napoleon died in 1821; the painting celebrates a popular revolt, not his empire.

options: (A) It depicts the storming of the Bastille in Paris in July of 1789.
(B) It commemorates the July Revolution of 1830 that overthrew Charles X, with Liberty personified as a woman leading the people, a common source of confusion with 1789.
(C) It was painted to celebrate the revolution of 1848 in Paris.
(D) It celebrates the military triumphs of Napoleon's empire, glorifying the emperor's conquests across Europe and portraying Liberty as the spirit of French imperial expansion.
stem: Which event does this painting actually commemorate, and why is that significant for interpreting it?
stimulus: Delacroix's 'Liberty Leading the People' (1830): a bare-breasted woman wearing a Phrygian cap and holding the French tricolor in one hand and a musket in the other strides over a barricade of rubble and fallen bodies, leading armed men forward — a boy with pistols at her side, a top-hatted rifleman behind.

explanation: The sketch shows 1848 as street warfare — citizens and soldiers fighting over improvised barricades — the revolutionary wave that shook nearly all of Europe.

option_explanations.A: The sketch is dated 1848, not 1789.
option_explanations.B: The fighting is in city streets among buildings, not in the countryside.
option_explanations.C: Both sides are shown fighting; the insurgents resist rather than collapse.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The barricade combat shows 1848 as mass urban insurrection spreading across European capitals.

options: (A) It shows the famous 1789 storming of the Bastille, when the Parisian crowd destroyed the royal fortress and seized its gunpowder stores.
(B) It depicts a rural peasant revolt.
(C) It shows government troops facing no resistance.
(D) The 1848 revolutions brought mass urban insurrection, ordinary people building barricades and fighting troops in the streets.
stem: What does this image reveal about the character of the 1848 revolutions?
stimulus: A pencil sketch of an 1848 attack on a Paris barricade: soldiers and insurgents exchange musket fire across a heap of rubble, paving stones, and overturned carts while figures fall in the street.

explanation: The lithograph's dead bodies, fallen horse, and advancing troops show 1848's human cost — popular uprisings fought with improvised street fortifications, not just parliamentary debates.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The casualties and rubble show 1848 as violent urban revolt, with citizens turning city streets into battlefields.
option_explanations.B: The bodies and fighting show violence, not peace.
option_explanations.C: The dress and 1848 caption place it in revolutionary Paris, not Napoleon's wars.
option_explanations.D: The street setting is urban Paris, not rural France.

options: (A) The 1848 uprisings were fought as violent urban revolts, with ordinary people building barricades and suffering heavy casualties.
(B) It shows a peaceful demonstration.
(C) It depicts one of Napoleon's early victories over the Austrian army in northern Italy during his famous campaigns of 1796 and 1797.
(D) It shows a revolt in rural France.
stem: What does this image show about how the 1848 revolution was fought?
stimulus: An 1848 lithograph of a Paris barricade: bodies lie among rubble and a fallen horse while soldiers advance past a tangle of paving stones, beams, and overturned carts that block the street.

explanation: Henri Christophe's palace — built by a formerly enslaved man turned king — used European royal architecture to declare Haiti's sovereignty and Black statehood legitimate.

option_explanations.A: The palace was built after independence by Haiti's own king, not by colonists.
option_explanations.B: It was a royal residence, not a military fort.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The grand European-style palace asserted that independent Haiti was a legitimate sovereign state ruled by Black monarchs.
option_explanations.D: Sans-Souci was built in the 1810s, not the 1500s.

options: (A) It was built by French colonists as a plantation great house before the revolution began, serving as the elegant residence of a wealthy white planter family.
(B) It is a French colonial military fort constructed to defend the harbor from attack.
(C) Haiti's early leaders built European-style palaces to assert the sovereignty and legitimacy of the new Black-ruled state after independence.
(D) It was built in the 1500s by the first Spanish settlers on the island.
stem: What does this building reveal about Haiti after independence?
stimulus: A modern photograph of the ruined Sans-Souci Palace in Haiti: the grand stone shell of a multi-story palace with arched windows stands on a green hillside, its roofless walls open to the sky.

explanation: The legend shows three forces — French (blue), Anglo-Dutch (red), Prussian (black) — converging June 16–18, with the Prussians arriving from the east at Waterloo on the 18th: a coalition victory, and reading the map is required to see it.

option_explanations.A: The 'Allied victory' marker at Waterloo on June 18 shows Napoleon lost.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The legend's three colored forces and dated arrows show a multinational coalition — including the Prussian arrival from the east — defeating Napoleon together.
option_explanations.C: The legend explicitly includes Prussian movements in black; they are essential to the outcome.
option_explanations.D: The legend dates the campaign June 16–18, 1815.

options: (A) Napoleon won the battle of Waterloo.
(B) Napoleon was defeated by a coalition of European powers, with Prussian troops arriving from the east at Waterloo on June 18, as the map's legend shows.
(C) Only French and British forces fought; no other powers were involved.
(D) The battle of Waterloo was fought in 1814, a full year before Napoleon's final abdication and his permanent exile to the remote island of St. Helena in the South Atlantic.
stem: A student reads this campaign map carefully, including its legend. Which conclusion is best supported?
stimulus: A campaign map of Waterloo with a detailed legend: blue arrows trace French movements, red arrows Anglo-Dutch movements, and black dashed arrows Prussian movements, dated June 16 through June 18; an 'Allied victory' marker sits at Waterloo on the 18th, with Prussian arrows arriving from the east.

explanation: The young General Bonaparte engraving captures the revolutionary career path: the wars let talented officers rise by merit, and French armies carried revolutionary reforms — and Napoleonic rule — across Europe.

option_explanations.A: Napoleon was a Corsican artillery officer who seized power; he inherited no throne.
option_explanations.B: The caption says 'General,' and the uniform is a general's — he became emperor only in 1804.
option_explanations.C: He was a product of the revolution who then buried the republic.
option_explanations.D: Correct. His rise through the revolutionary armies shows how the wars created new avenues of advancement and spread French power and reforms across Europe.

options: (A) He inherited the French throne from his father.
(B) The image shows him already crowned as emperor, wearing splendid imperial robes and holding the symbols of imperial power at his grand coronation ceremony.
(C) He opposed the French Revolution from the beginning.
(D) The revolutionary wars let talented officers rise by merit, and French armies spread revolutionary reforms and Napoleon's rule across Europe.
stem: What does Napoleon's early career, shown here, illustrate about the revolutionary era?
stimulus: An engraving captioned 'GENERAL BONAPARTE': a young officer in a French general's uniform with epaulettes gazes out, his hair long in the style of the 1790s.

explanation: The ambush scene shows Haitians using dense tropical forest for cover — the same environment whose yellow fever killed tens of thousands of French troops, making disease and terrain decisive allies of the revolution.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The jungle setting shows how Haitians exploited terrain and climate — and the diseases it bred — against European armies.
option_explanations.B: The Haitian fighters are attacking, not surrendering.
option_explanations.C: The fighting is hand-to-hand on land, not at sea.
option_explanations.D: The French lost the war; their numbers and weapons did not save them.

options: (A) Haiti's tropical terrain and disease devastated European armies, making geography and climate decisive allies of the revolution.
(B) The image shows Haitian forces surrendering to the French.
(C) It depicts a naval battle between Haitian and French ships.
(D) European armies won in Haiti because of their superior numbers, better weapons, professional military discipline, and naval support.
stem: What role does the environment shown here play in explaining the Haitian Revolution's outcome?
stimulus: A 19th-century engraving of fighting in the Haitian Revolution: Black Haitian fighters ambush European soldiers in dense tropical forest, grappling hand-to-hand among thick vegetation while others fire from cover.

explanation: Tegg's 1807 cartoon satirizes the blockade war: Napoleon's Continental System versus Britain's naval blockade. The well-fed John Bull implies British commercial and naval strength would outlast French economic warfare.

option_explanations.A: No battle is shown; the weapons are a 'wall of blockade' and rival dinners.
option_explanations.B: The two figures glare at each other across a blockade wall — rivals, not allies.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The cartoon mocks the rival blockades and uses John Bull's roast beef versus Napoleon's 'soupe maigre' to claim Britain's economy would win the economic war.
option_explanations.D: Tegg was a London publisher; the cartoon is pro-British propaganda.

options: (A) The cartoon shows a land battle between British and French armies fighting on a battlefield.

(B) It depicts a formal military alliance between Britain and Napoleonic France against Russia, showing John Bull and Napoleon setting aside their rivalry to feast together as partners in a new coalition against the Russian Empire.

(C) Britain and France waged economic warfare through rival blockades, Napoleon's Continental System against Britain's naval blockade, and British propaganda claimed Britain's strength would outlast France.
(D) It was published by the French government to celebrate Napoleon's economic policies.
stem: What conflict does this cartoon satirize?
stimulus: Thomas Tegg's 1807 cartoon 'Blockade against Blockade, or John Bull a Match for Boney': John Bull peers over a wall labeled with blockade orders at a glum Napoleon eating a thin 'soupe maigre,' while Bull enjoys a hearty roast-beef dinner on his side of the wall.

explanation: The cartoon visualizes the Cape-to-Cairo ambition: Rhodes striding the length of Africa with a telegraph line symbolizes Britain's goal of an unbroken chain of territory from south to north. This ambition was a major driver of the Scramble for Africa, putting Britain in direct competition with France, Portugal, and others for the same ground.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. No trans-African railway was ever completed; the cartoon shows an ambition, not an accomplished fact. Reading aspiration as achievement is the common error here.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the image shows African resistance; the figure dominates the map unopposed, which is precisely the imperial fantasy the cartoon celebrates.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Rhodes was the foremost promoter of British expansion in southern Africa; the cartoon praises, not criticizes, his imperialism.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The stride from Cape Town to Cairo and the telegraph wire depict the aspiration for continuous British territory and communications across Africa, a central motive of the Scramble for Africa.

options: (A) The completion of a British-built railway running the full length of Africa by 1892, presented here as a finished triumph of imperial engineering
(B) African rulers' successful resistance to European railway and telegraph projects, which forced Rhodes to abandon his plans
(C) Rhodes's campaign to persuade the British government to abandon imperial expansion in Africa and withdraw
(D) Britain's drive to connect its African possessions in one continuous north-south corridor, intensifying rivalry with other European powers
stem: This cartoon was published to celebrate Rhodes's ambition. Which development in late nineteenth-century imperialism does it best illustrate?
stimulus: A British political cartoon from Punch magazine, December 1892, titled "The Rhodes Colossus." It shows the businessman and imperialist Cecil Rhodes as a giant striding across the map of Africa, one foot planted at Cape Town in the south and the other reaching toward Cairo in the north. In his right hand he holds a telegraph wire stretching behind him, and a caption beneath reads: "STRIDING FROM CAPE TOWN TO CAIRO."

explanation: The cartoon shows Leopold carving up the Congo as the other powers merely watch, and the caption's sarcastic question about when "the peoples" will feast points out that Africans got nothing. It criticizes the gap between the conference's humanitarian rhetoric and its real result: legitimizing Leopold's personal control of the Congo, where forced labor would later cause millions of deaths.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The cartoon shows Leopold as the one doing the carving; he was the chief beneficiary of the conference's Congo settlement, not its opponent.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The conference did the opposite: it set rules for recognizing colonial claims, which accelerated the partition rather than stopping it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The image depicts Leopold dividing the Congo before passive onlookers, and the caption mocks the idea that ordinary Africans benefited, capturing the hypocrisy critics saw in the conference.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No African representatives attended the Berlin Conference; the cartoon's point is exactly that Africans were carved up without any voice.

options: (A) That Leopold II opposed the partition of Africa and worked to protect Congolese sovereignty against the other European powers
(B) That the conference outlawed all European colonial claims in Africa and ordered the powers to withdraw from the continent
(C) That the conference let Leopold II personally seize the Congo while the other powers watched, despite their talk of uplift and reform
(D) That African rulers were given an equal seat at the conference table, negotiating the partition of their own continent alongside the Europeans
stem: What criticism is the cartoonist making about the Berlin Conference and its outcome?
stimulus: A French political cartoon published around the time of the Berlin Conference (1884-1885). It shows King Leopold II of Belgium slicing open a large sack labeled "CONGO" that lies spread across a map labeled "AFRIQUE." A lion, symbolizing Britain, and a figure labeled "ALLEMAGNE" (Germany) look on from the side. The caption asks, in French: "A QUAND LE REVEILLON DES PEUPLES?" ("When will the peoples have their New Year's feast?")

explanation: The cartoon visualizes Kipling's "civilizing mission" argument: the rocks' labels present colonized peoples as weighed down by ignorance and barbarism, while the straining carriers and the shining goal of "CIVILIZATION" frame empire as a heavy but noble responsibility rather than mere conquest.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The cartoon deliberately avoids money motives and stresses moral duty instead, which is why it was such an effective ideological cover for economic interests.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Every element, the burdened carriers, the labeled rocks, the distant goal, presents empire as a duty to uplift supposedly inferior peoples, the classic civilizing-mission justification.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. This misreads the cartoon's stance: it endorses the burden as noble, not condemnable. Anti-imperialists existed, but this image is not theirs.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The cartoon's whole visual logic depends on depicting the colonized as uncivilized figures needing to be carried; it never suggests they were already civilized.

options: (A) That economic profit was the only motive anyone ever publicly claimed for building an empire
(B) That empire is a moral duty: superior nations must carry backward peoples upward toward civilization
(C) That imperialism is simple theft, and that the cartoon condemns Britain and America for stealing colonies
(D) That colonized peoples were already fully civilized and therefore needed no outside help at all
stem: Which justification for imperialism does this cartoon promote?
stimulus: An 1899 American cartoon from Judge magazine titled "The White Man's Burden," subtitled "(Apology to Rudyard Kipling)." It shows John Bull (Britain) and Uncle Sam (the United States) each carrying a large basket of dark-skinned figures, one labeled "CUBA," up a steep slope of rocks labeled "OPPRESSION," "IGNORANCE," "BARBARISM," and "SUPERSTITION" toward a distant figure labeled "CIVILIZATION."

explanation: The photograph shows the Meiji strategy of selective borrowing: officials adopted Western dress, institutions, and technology (the mission studied Western governments, schools, and industry for two years) precisely to strengthen Japan and end the unequal treaties, while retaining Japanese sovereignty and identity. The seated leader's kimono alongside Western suits makes the selectivity visible.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Adopting Western dress and institutions was a deliberate state strategy, not a loss of culture; the mission's goal was to strengthen, not surrender, Japanese sovereignty.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. This is the opposite error: the mission existed precisely because Japan wanted to learn from the West in order to renegotiate the unequal treaties.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Japan was never colonized in this period; the officials wear Western dress by choice as part of a state-directed reform program.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The two-year Iwakura Mission toured the United States and Europe studying Western systems, and the mixed dress in the photo captures the policy: adopt Western tools, keep Japanese control.

options: (A) The total abandonment of Japanese culture in a deliberate, state-directed effort to remake Japan as a Western nation
(B) Japan's complete refusal to engage with the Western world at any level in the decades after the Meiji Restoration
(C) Japan's status as a European colony, with its officials dressed in Western clothes and posed for the camera by their colonial rulers in Tokyo
(D) Selective borrowing from the West: Meiji officials studied Western institutions abroad so Japan could industrialize and resist colonization
stem: This photograph shows members of the Iwakura Mission (1871-1873). What does it suggest about the Meiji government's approach to reform?
stimulus: A photograph of five Japanese officials of the Iwakura Mission taken while they toured the United States and Europe in 1871-1873. Four of the men wear Western business suits and hold top hats; the seated leader, Iwakura Tomomi, wears a traditional Japanese kimono with his topknot hairstyle.

explanation: Beato, one of the first war photographers, documented the aftermath of the rebellion for British audiences. The public hanging of captured sepoys, photographed and circulated, shows how Britain answered the 1857 uprising: with exemplary terror meant to deter further resistance and to demonstrate that imperial authority had been restored. The image is itself an instrument of that message.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The public execution of rebels, deliberately photographed, shows Britain reimposing control through exemplary punishment and using the new medium of photography to broadcast that control.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The British response was overwhelmingly punitive, mass executions, reprisals, and the end of the East India Company's rule, not negotiation.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The rebels did not have access to or use photography this way; the photographer, Felice Beato, traveled with and documented the British campaign.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The rebellion was massive and nearly toppled British rule in northern India; this photograph documents the punishment that followed its suppression, not an absence of fighting.

options: (A) Britain responded with public, exemplary punishment, and it used the new technology of photography to display restored imperial authority
(B) By negotiating a compromise settlement that preserved the Mughal emperor's throne and addressed the sepoys' long-standing grievances about pay, cartridges, and promotions
(C) The photograph was made by rebel leaders to rally further resistance against British rule across northern India
(D) There was almost no fighting during 1857, so the British authorities had very little to respond to
stem: Felice Beato was one of the first war photographers. What does the existence and circulation of this photograph reveal about the British response to the 1857 rebellion?
